column2: When you know me, O lord of gods, to be a fit vessel for bearing weapons, then I serve you, and you ought to give me weapons.
[Duryodhana said:] Then he, with austerity, self-control and discipline, with offerings of worship, oblations and sacrifices led by mantras,
worshipped Sharva for many years, and Mahadeva was pleased with the great-souled Bhargava.
He spoke many times of his virtues in the presence of the Goddess: "This Rama is ever devoted to me, firm in his vows."
Thus, pleased, the Lord, slayer of foes, often told of his virtues in the presence of gods and fathers.
At that very time there were mighty daityas, who then, blinded by pride and delusion, harassed the dwellers in heaven.
Then the gods, assembling, resolved to slay them, exerted themselves to kill their foes, but could not conquer them.
Then the gods went to Maheshvara and, propitiating him with devotion, said, "Slay the hosts of foes."
Having promised to destroy the gods' enemies, the god Shankara summoned Rama Bhargava and said:
Bhargava, slay all the assembled foes of the gods, for the sake of the good of the worlds and out of regard for me.
[Rama said:] "O lord of gods, Maheshvara, what strength have I, unskilled in weapons, to slay all the danavas, skilled in weapons and arrogant in battle?"
[Ishvara said:] "Go; by meditation on me you will slay the danavas; having conquered all foes you will gain abundant virtues."
[Duryodhana said:] Hearing these words and accepting them fully, Rama, having performed auspicious rites, went against the danavas.
Bhargava slew those enemies of the gods, filled with intoxication, pride and strength, with blows touching like thunderbolts.
Jamadagni's son, best of the twice-born, with his body wounded by the danavas, was touched by Sthanu and at once became free of wounds.
The Lord God, pleased with that deed of his, gave boons to the great-souled Bhargava, the knower of Brahman.
The god of gods, the trident-bearer, full of affection, said: "The pain that arose in your body from the falling of weapons,
by that your human act has been done away with, scion of Bhrigu. Take divine weapons from me as you wish."
Having then obtained all the weapons and various boons desired in mind, Rama, bowing his head to Shiva,
obtained the leave of the lord of gods and that greatly ascetic one went away. Thus the sage then told this ancient tale.
And Bhargava gave the whole science of the bow to the great-souled Karna, tiger among men, with a very pleased heart.
If there had been any fault in Karna, O king, the scion of Bhrigu would not have given him divine weapons.

See his plump arms like the trunks of elephant-kings, see his broad chest that slays all foes."
A hero superior to the chariot-warrior should be made the chariot's driver; therefore, tiger among men, rein in the horses in the battle.
[Sanjaya said:] Then Shalya, embracing your son, said to Duryodhana, slayer of foes, the king of the Madras being pleased:

If you think so, O king, son of Gandhari, pleasing to behold, then whatever is pleasing to you I shall do all of it.

[Sanjaya said:] Then Duryodhana again said to the mighty king of the Madras, who was reining the best horses in the battle, O king:
Protected by you, Radheya will conquer Dhananjaya. Thus addressed, he mounted the chariot and said "So be it," O Bharata.

These and many other very dreadful portents arose there, O revered one, for the destruction of the Kauravas.
All of them, bewildered by fate, did not heed them; men on earth cried "Victory!" to the departing charioteer's son, and your Kauravas thought the Pandavas already conquered.
